questions.stem:
In the presence of air resistance, a cyclist and his bicycle of total mass 80.0 kg is able to coast down a smooth slope at a constant speed of 1.4 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ as shown below.

The air resistance is directly proportional to the cyclist’s speed.

What is the additional force that the cyclist must apply in order to descend the same slope at a steady speed of 5.5 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$?
questions.stemText: In the presence of air resistance, a cyclist and his bicycle of total mass 80.0 kg is able to coast down a smooth slope at a constant speed of 1.4 m s–1 as shown below. 5° The air resistance is directly proportional to the cyclist’s speed. What is the additional force that the cyclist must apply in order to descend the same slope at a steady speed of 5.5 m s–1? A 200 N B 340 N C 2200 N D 3800 N

appearances.originalFile: grail:9605 ACJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must use force balance at both speeds and scale the drag between them.
questions.misconception: Adding gravity and drag as if they act in the same direction

explanation.body: At $1.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, air resistance balances the downhill component of weight, so $1.4k=(80.0)(9.81)\sin 5^\circ$ and $k=48.857\ \mathrm{N\,s\,m^{-1}}$. At $5.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the air resistance is $(5.5)(48.857)=268.71\ \mathrm N$. The additional downhill force is $268.71-(80.0)(9.81)\sin5^\circ=200\ \mathrm N$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Adds the downhill weight component to the uphill drag magnitude.
perOption.C: Using the full weight in place of its downslope component inflates the calculated drag and the required force.
perOption.D: Using nearly the full weight to infer the drag and then adding gravity instead of subtracting it inflates the result further.

[Blocks X, Y and Z touch in that order from left to right on a smooth horizontal surface. A rightward arrow labelled $F$ points at the left face of X.]

What is the force exerted on Y by X?

A $\frac{1}{6}F$
B $\frac{1}{2}F$
C $\frac{5}{6}F$
D $F$

stemImage.alt: Question 6: Three blocks X, Y and Z of masses m, 2m and 3m respectively, are accelerated along a smooth horizontal surface by a force F applied to block X as shown in the d

appearances.originalFile: grail:9605 ACJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must apply Newton’s laws to the whole system and to one block in isolation.
questions.misconception: Confusing the net force on a block with the contact force

explanation.body: For X, Y and Z together, $F=6ma$. For X alone, $F-F_{Y\to X}=ma$, so $F_{Y\to X}=5ma=\tfrac56F$. By Newton’s third law, the force of X on Y has the same magnitude.

perOption.A: Gives the resultant force on X.
perOption.B: Gives the contact force accelerating Z alone.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assigns the entire applied force to the contact even though X also accelerates.

questions.difficultyReason: Students must translate the force profile into the changing slope of a speed graph.
questions.misconception: Reading force as speed.

explanation.body: Assuming the force acts along the initial motion, $a=F/m$ gives the gradient of the speed–time graph. The speed stays constant at first, rises with an increasingly steep gradient as the force grows, and stays constant at its new value once the force drops to zero.

perOption.A: Correct. It shows a progressively steeper rise followed by constant speed.
perOption.B: Its straight rising segment implies constant force.
perOption.C: Its final decline requires a backward force after the applied force ends.
perOption.D: Its instantaneous speed jump requires a finite impulse delivered in zero time.

What is the ratio $\dfrac{\text{distance travelled between 0 s to 10 s}}{\text{distance travelled between 0 s to 5 s}}$?

A  1.2
B  1.3
C  1.5
D  1.8

questions.difficultyReason: Students need to compare a triangle and a trapezium on a speed–time graph.
questions.misconception: Using the speed at one instant in place of the area.

explanation.body: Distance is the area under the speed–time graph. The triangle from 5 to 10 s has half the base and half the height of the whole triangle, so it covers one quarter of the total area. The first 5 s therefore account for three quarters of the total distance, giving a ratio of $4/3\approx 1.3$.

perOption.A: It underestimates the contribution of the last 5 s.
perOption.B: Correct. The first 5 s cover three quarters of the total distance.
perOption.C: It overestimates the last 5 s by treating its distance as half the first interval’s.
perOption.D: It assigns almost as much distance to the last 5 s as to the first despite the much lower speed.

Which of the following cannot be the magnitude of its final speed?
questions.stemText: A 3.0 kg block is moving on a smooth surface with a speed of 2.0 m s–1. A constant force of 1.5 N is exerted on the block over 2.0 s in a fixed direction. Which of the following cannot be the magnitude of its final speed? A 0.5 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ B 1.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ C 2.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ D 3.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:10416 ACJC 2023 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must calculate the velocity change and then find the range of possible vector sums.
questions.misconception: Treating change in velocity as a scalar.

explanation.body: The force changes the velocity by a vector of magnitude $Ft/m=(1.5)(2.0)/3.0=1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The final speed is smallest when this change opposes the initial velocity and largest when it points along it. It can range from $1.0$ to $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so $0.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is impossible.

perOption.A: Correct. It is below the minimum final speed.
perOption.B: This is possible when the force opposes the initial velocity.
perOption.C: This is possible with a force angled so the final velocity has the original magnitude.
perOption.D: This is possible when the force points along the initial velocity.

What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the block?

The tension in the string is 2.0 N and the frictional force exerted by the slope is 3.0 N. What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the block? A 3.9 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ B 5.1 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ C 5.9 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ D 7.5 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:10416 ACJC 2023 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must resolve the weight and assign signs to both forces along the slope.
questions.misconception: Assigning friction the same direction as the downhill motion.

explanation.body: The component of weight down the slope is $mg\sin30^\circ$. The block slides down the slope, so both tension and friction act uphill. Newton’s second law gives $a=(5.0g\sin30^\circ-2.0-3.0)/5.0=3.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ down the slope.

perOption.A: Correct. Both tension and friction reduce the downhill resultant.
perOption.B: Adds friction downslope while subtracting tension.
perOption.C: Adds both friction and tension to the downhill weight component.
perOption.D: Uses the perpendicular weight component $mg\cos30^\circ$ in the along-slope equation.

questions.stemText:
A block is released from rest down a frictionless inclined plane of angle $\theta$. The block passes two light sensors $\mathrm{S_1}$ and $\mathrm{S_2}$ at time $t_1$ and $t_2$ respectively.

[The block is uphill of $\mathrm{S_1}$ on a plane sloping down to the right at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. $\mathrm{S_2}$ is farther downhill. Two dashed lines perpendicular to the slope mark the sensor positions, separated by distance $h$ along the slope.]

What is the acceleration of free fall?

A $\frac{2h}{t_2^2-t_1^2}$
B $\frac{2h}{(t_2-t_1)^2}$
C $\frac{2h}{(t_2^2-t_1^2)\cos\theta}$
D $\frac{2h}{(t_2^2-t_1^2)\sin\theta}$

stemImage.alt: Question 3: A block is released from rest down a frictionless inclined plane of angle . The block passes two light sensors S1 and S2 at time t1 and t2 respectively. What i

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation requires comparing two displacements from release and resolving gravity along the incline.
questions.misconception: Treating the block as stationary at the first sensor.

explanation.body: Use $s=ut+\frac12at^2$ with $u=0$ at release. Subtracting the two displacements gives $h=\frac12a(t_2^2-t_1^2)$, so $a=\frac{2h}{t_2^2-t_1^2}$. Since $a=g\sin\theta$, $g=\frac{2h}{(t_2^2-t_1^2)\sin\theta}$.

perOption.A: Gives the acceleration along the incline.
perOption.B: Uses $(t_2-t_1)^2$ as if the block started from rest at the first sensor.
perOption.C: Uses $\cos\theta$, the factor for the component perpendicular to the slope.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A toy rocket consists of a plastic bottle which is partially filled with water as shown in the figure below. The space above the water contains compressed air.

[An upright bottle with fins has compressed air above the water and a nozzle at the bottom.]

At one instant during the flight of the rocket bottle, water of density $1000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ is forced out of the nozzle of radius $0.012\ \mathrm{m}$ at a speed of $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ relative to the nozzle.

What is the rate of change of momentum of the water?

A $45\ \mathrm{N}$
B $120\ \mathrm{N}$
C $3800\ \mathrm{N}$
D $7500\ \mathrm{N}$

stemImage.alt: Question 4: A toy rocket consists of a plastic bottle which is partially filled with water as shown in the figure below. The space above the water contains compressed air.

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must turn a volume flow rate into a mass flow rate and then into a momentum rate.
questions.misconception: Confusing mass flow rate with momentum flow rate.

explanation.body: The rate of change of momentum is $v\frac{\Delta m}{t}$, where $v$ is the water speed relative to the nozzle. In time $t$, a column of water of length $h$ passes through the nozzle, giving $\Delta m=\rho\pi r^2h$. Since $h/t=v$, the momentum rate is $\rho\pi r^2v^2=1000\pi(0.012)^2(10)^2\approx45\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Using the radius directly in place of $\pi r^2$ and counting the speed only once gives 120 but has the wrong units.
perOption.C: Uses $\pi r$ in place of the nozzle area $\pi r^2$.
perOption.D: Uses the circumference $2\pi r$ in place of the nozzle area $\pi r^2$.

questions.misconception: Treating final velocity as the change in velocity.

explanation.body: The speed is constant, so $|\mathbf v_f|=|\mathbf v_i|$. Draw $\Delta\mathbf v=\mathbf v_f+(-\mathbf v_i)$ by adding the down-right final velocity to the leftward reverse of the initial velocity. The resultant points steeply down and left.

perOption.B: Points up and left even though the vertical change is downward.

questions.stem:
A transport system used to move luggage from the airport terminal to the aircraft consists of a powered vehicle connected to four baggage carts by a series of connecting bars.

The mass of each of the baggage carts is 400 kg and the system starts with an acceleration of 2.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$.

Ignore any frictional forces on the carts.

What is the tension in the connecting bar between baggage carts 2 and 3?
questions.stemText: A transport system used to move luggage from the airport terminal to the aircraft consists of a powered vehicle connected to four baggage carts by a series of connecting bars. The mass of each of the baggage carts is 400 kg and the system starts with an acceleration of 2.0 m s–2. Ignore any frictional forces on the carts. What is the tension in the connecting bar between baggage carts 2 and 3? A 400 N B 800 N C 1200 N D 1600 N

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation is direct once the two trailing carts are treated as one system.
questions.misconception: Choosing the wrong carts for the system.

explanation.body: Treat carts 3 and 4 as one system of mass $800\ \mathrm{kg}$. The bar tension $T$ is the only external horizontal force on this system. By $F=ma$, $T=800(2.0)=1600\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: Uses the mass of one cart as the force without applying the acceleration.
perOption.B: Uses the mass of only one trailing cart in $F=ma$.
perOption.C: Uses $600\ \mathrm{kg}$ in $F=ma$ even though the two trailing carts total $800\ \mathrm{kg}$.
perOption.D: Correct. The tension accelerates both trailing carts.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A child of mass m sits on a car seat which is accelerating horizontally at 0.50 g (where g is the acceleration of free fall).

What is the magnitude of the total force F exerted by the car seat on the child?
questions.stemText: A child of mass m sits on a car seat which is accelerating horizontally at 0.50 g (where g is the acceleration of free fall). F What is the magnitude of the total force F exerted by the car seat on the child? A 0.50 mg B 1.0 mg C 1.1 mg D 1.5 mg

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires seeing that the seat supplies both the vertical support and the horizontal accelerating force, then combining vectors.
questions.misconception: Taking only the horizontal or only the vertical component of the contact force

explanation.body:
For vertical equilibrium, $F_y = mg$. For horizontal motion, $F_x = ma = 0.50\,mg$.

$F = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2} = \sqrt{(0.50mg)^2 + (mg)^2} = 1.1\,mg$.

perOption.A: Only the horizontal component $F_x$; ignores supporting the weight.
perOption.B: Only the vertical component $F_y$; ignores the acceleration.
perOption.C: Correct. Vector sum of the two perpendicular components.
perOption.D: Adds the components as scalars instead of as vectors.

questions.stem: A car is travelling at constant velocity. Its brakes are then applied, causing uniform deceleration. Which graph shows the variation with distance s of the velocity v of the car?
questions.stemText: A car is travelling at constant velocity. Its brakes are then applied, causing uniform deceleration. Which graph shows the variation with distance s of the velocity v of the car? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: grail:9611 ASRJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must distinguish a velocity–distance graph from a velocity–time graph.
questions.misconception: Treating uniform deceleration as a constant slope on any velocity graph.

explanation.body: Before braking, $v$ is constant. During braking, $v^2=u^2+2as$, with $a$ constant and negative and $s$ measured from the start of braking. Thus $v=\sqrt{u^2+2as}$, which falls increasingly steeply as the car comes to rest.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats uniform deceleration as a constant gradient on a velocity–distance graph.
perOption.C: Shows the curve flattening as the speed falls, whereas its gradient grows steeper.
perOption.D: Shows an instantaneous drop in velocity, which requires more than a finite deceleration.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A ball strikes a horizontal surface with momentum $p$ at an angle $\theta$ to the surface, as shown.

[The incoming momentum arrow $p$ points down and right toward the horizontal surface. The outgoing momentum arrow $p$ points up and right away from the same point. Each path makes angle $\theta$ with the surface.]

The ball rebounds with the same magnitude of momentum at an angle $\theta$ to the surface.

The ball is in contact with the surface for time $t$.

What is the magnitude of the average resultant force acting on the ball during the collision?

A zero
B $\frac{2p}{t}$
C $\frac{2p\cos\theta}{t}$
D $\frac{2p\sin\theta}{t}$

stemImage.alt: Question 5: A ball strikes a horizontal surface with momentum p at an angle θ to the surface, as shown. The ball rebounds with the same magnitude of momentum at an angle θ

appearances.originalFile: grail:9611 ASRJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must resolve both momentum vectors and track which signed component reverses.
questions.misconception: Treating momentum change as the change in momentum magnitude.

explanation.body: The horizontal change in momentum is $p\cos\theta-p\cos\theta=0$, so the average horizontal force is zero. Taking upward as positive, the vertical change is $p\sin\theta-(-p\sin\theta)=2p\sin\theta$. Dividing by the contact time gives an average resultant force of magnitude $2p\sin\theta/t$.

perOption.A: Confuses equal momentum magnitudes with an unchanged momentum vector.
perOption.B: Assumes the whole momentum vector reverses.
perOption.C: Uses the horizontal component, which is unchanged.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stem:
A sprinter takes a time of 11.0 s to run a 100 m race. She first accelerates uniformly from rest, reaching a speed of 10 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. She then runs at a constant speed of 10 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ until the finish line.

What is the uniform acceleration of the sprinter for the first part of the race?
questions.stemText: A sprinter takes a time of 11.0 s to run a 100 m race. She first accelerates uniformly from rest, reaching a speed of 10 m s-1. She then runs at a constant speed of 10 m s-1 until the finish line. What is the uniform acceleration of the sprinter for the first part of the race? A 0.5 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ B 0.91 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ C 1.7 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ D 5.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:12935 2023 ASRJC H2 physics Promo P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must use the total distance to infer the duration of the acceleration phase.
questions.misconception: Using total race time as acceleration time

explanation.body: Let $t$ be the time spent accelerating from rest. The distance is the trapezium area under the velocity–time graph, so $100=\frac{11.0+(11.0-t)}{2}\times10$. This gives $t=2.0\ \mathrm{s}$ and $a=10/t=5.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: This acceleration would take 20 s to reach the stated speed, longer than the race.
perOption.B: Divides the speed gain by the full 11.0 s, including the constant-speed phase.
perOption.C: This implies almost 6 s of acceleration and gives only about 81 m in 11.0 s.
perOption.D: Correct. The speed increases by 10 m/s over 2.0 s.

The blocks remain in contact as they accelerate along a horizontal frictionless surface. Air resistance is negligible. X has a greater mass than Y. Which statement is correct? A The acceleration of X is equal to force F divided by the mass of X. B The force that X exerts on Y is equal to F. C The force that X exerts on Y is less than F. questions.difficultyReason: The student must distinguish the applied force from the resultant force on X and use Newton’s third law.
questions.misconception: Treating the applied force as the resultant on X

explanation.body: The blocks stay in contact, so they have the same acceleration $a$. If $F_{YX}$ is the magnitude of the backward contact force on X, then $a=(F-F_{YX})/m_X$. perOption.B: If X exerted F on Y, Y would exert an equal opposing force on X, giving X zero acceleration.

perOption.D: The two contact forces form a Newton’s third-law pair and have equal magnitudes.

questions.stem:
A man is skiing down a slope with constant speed.

According to Newton’s third law, which force makes an action−reaction pair with the weight of the man?
questions.stemText: A man is skiing down a slope with constant speed. According to Newton’s third law, which force makes an action−reaction pair with the weight of the man? A the friction from the slope B the normal contact force from the slope C the gravitational force on the Earth due to the man D the sum of normal contact force and friction from the slope

options.label: B
options.text: the normal contact force from the slope

options.label: C
options.text: the gravitational force on the Earth due to the man

options.label: D
options.text: the sum of normal contact force and friction from the slope

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The skier's steady speed can distract students from identifying the second force in the gravitational interaction.
questions.misconception: Confusing balanced forces with a third-law pair.

explanation.body: An action–reaction pair consists of forces of the same type. The man's weight is the gravitational force exerted by Earth on him, so its partner is the gravitational force he exerts on Earth.

perOption.A: Friction is a contact force exerted on the man by the slope.
perOption.B: The normal force is a contact force exerted on the man by the slope.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The sum may balance the weight, but both contact forces act on the man.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The diagram shows a laboratory experiment in which a feather falls from rest in a long evacuated vertical tube of length L.

The feather takes time T to fall from the top to the bottom of the tube.

How far does the feather fall from the top of the tube in time 0.50T?
questions.stemText: The diagram shows a laboratory experiment in which a feather falls from rest in a long evacuated vertical tube of length L. The feather takes time T to fall from the top to the bottom of the tube. How far does the feather fall from the top of the tube in time 0.50T? A 0.13L B 0.25L C 0.38L D 0.50L

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: The student must use the square of the time ratio for free fall from rest.
questions.misconception: Assuming distance is proportional to time

explanation.body: Use $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$ with $u=0$ and constant $a$, so $s\propto t^2$. If $x$ is the distance fallen in $0.50T$, then $x/L=(0.50T)^2/T^2=0.25$, giving $x=0.25L$.

perOption.A: Keeps an extra factor of one-half when taking the ratio, although that factor cancels.
perOption.B: Correct. Halving the time quarters the distance.
perOption.C: The distance is fixed by the squared time ratio, which gives $0.25L$.
perOption.D: Assumes constant speed and takes the distance to be proportional to time.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The graph shows the variation of velocity with time for a stone that falls from a bridge into a lake and sinks to the bottom of the lake.

What can be deduced about the motion of the stone?
questions.stemText: The graph shows the variation of velocity with time for a stone that falls from a bridge into a lake and sinks to the bottom of the lake. What can be deduced about the motion of the stone? A Terminal velocity was reached in air. B The distance travelled in water was greater than the distance travelled in air. C The acceleration in air was decreasing with increasing time. D The rate of change of velocity in air was constant.

options.label: A
options.text: Terminal velocity was reached in air.

options.label: B
options.text: The distance travelled in water was greater than the distance travelled in air.

options.label: C
options.text: The acceleration in air was decreasing with increasing time.

options.label: D
options.text: The rate of change of velocity in air was constant.

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: The student must identify the air and water sections and interpret both their slopes and areas.
questions.misconception: Confusing height or duration with area on a velocity–time graph

explanation.body: The horizontal section shows that the stone reaches terminal velocity in water. The area under the graph in air is larger than the area in water, so the stone travels farther in air. The gradient in air decreases with time, so the acceleration in air also decreases.

perOption.A: The air section still has a positive slope at water entry.
perOption.B: The area under the water section is smaller than the area under the air section.
perOption.C: Correct. The slope decreases during the fall through air.
perOption.D: A constant rate of change would give a straight line in air.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A box rests on the Earth with forces P, Q, R, S and T acting on them as shown. Newton’s third law describes how forces of the same type act in pairs.

Which of the following correctly identifies the pair of forces?
questions.stemText: A box rests on the Earth with forces P, Q, R, S and T acting on them as shown. Newton’s third law describes how forces of the same type act in pairs. P T S R Q Which of the following correctly identifies the pair of forces? A P and S B P and Q C P and R D R and Q

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: The student must identify the interaction and the body on which each force acts.
questions.misconception: Pairing forces that balance on the same object

explanation.body: A Newton’s third-law pair consists of forces of the same type that act in opposite directions on different bodies. $P$ is the upward contact force of Earth on the box, and $R$ is the downward contact force of the box on Earth.

perOption.A: Both act on the box, and one is a contact force while the other is gravitational.
perOption.B: Both point upward and come from different interactions.
perOption.C: Correct. They are the mutual contact forces.
perOption.D: Pairs a contact force with a gravitational force.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Water is pumped through a hosepipe at a rate of 90 kg per minute. It emerges from the hosepipe horizontally with a speed of 20 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

Which force is required from a person holding the hosepipe to prevent it moving backwards?
questions.stemText: Water is pumped through a hosepipe at a rate of 90 kg per minute. It emerges from the hosepipe horizontally with a speed of 20 m s–1. Which force is required from a person holding the hosepipe to prevent it moving backwards? A 30 N B 270 N C 1800 N D 10800 N

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: The student must convert the flow rate and use the rate of change of momentum as a force.
questions.misconception: Using mass per minute as mass per second

explanation.body: The mass flow rate is $90\ \mathrm{kg\,min^{-1}}=1.5\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$. The horizontal rate of momentum transfer is $F=v\,\Delta m/\Delta t=20(1.5)=30\ \mathrm{N}$. The person applies this force in the direction of the jet to balance the backward reaction.

perOption.A: Correct. The jet carries away momentum at a rate of 30 N.
perOption.B: A force of 270 N would require a mass flow of 13.5 kg per second at the stated jet speed.
perOption.C: Uses 90 kg per minute as though it were 90 kg per second.
perOption.D: A force of 10,800 N would require using 540 kg per second, 360 times the actual mass flow.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two blocks of identical size, one made of wood and the other of copper, are at rest on the ground as shown in (1) and (2). Both blocks are then accelerated upwards by an applied force F as shown in (3).

Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.stemText: Two blocks of identical size, one made of wood and the other of copper, are at rest on the ground as shown in (1) and (2). Both blocks are then accelerated upwards by an applied force F as shown in (3). (3) (1) (2) copper wood wood copper copper wood force F ground ground ground Which of the following statements is correct? A The force by ground on the copper block in (1) is greater than the force by the ground on the wooden block in (2) because the copper block is denser than the wooden block and exerts a bigger force on the ground. B The force by the wooden block on the copper block in (1) is the same as that by the copper block on the wooden block in (2) due to Newton’s Third Law. C The force by the copper block on the wooden block in (3) is equal to that by the copper block on the wooden block in (2). D The applied force F on the wooden block in (3) is greater than the force by the ground on the copper block in (1).

options.label: A
options.text: The force by ground on the copper block in (1) is greater than the force by the ground on the wooden block in (2) because the copper block is denser than the wooden block and exerts a bigger force on the ground.

options.label: B
options.text: The force by the wooden block on the copper block in (1) is the same as that by the copper block on the wooden block in (2) due to Newton’s Third Law.

options.label: C
options.text: The force by the copper block on the wooden block in (3) is equal to that by the copper block on the wooden block in (2).

options.label: D
options.text: The applied force F on the wooden block in (3) is greater than the force by the ground on the copper block in (1).

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires careful free-body reasoning for stacked blocks at rest and accelerating, and correct identification of third-law pairs.
questions.misconception: Misidentifying Newton's third-law pairs and ignoring that acceleration changes contact forces

explanation.body: Treat the two blocks as one system. At rest, the ground’s upward force balances their combined weight. When the system accelerates upward in (3), the applied force must exceed that combined weight.

perOption.A: The ground supports the same combined weight in (1) and (2).
perOption.B: The third-law partner is the copper block’s force on the wooden block in (1), in the same configuration.
perOption.C: In (3), the wood’s upward force on the copper must exceed the copper’s weight, so the copper pushes down harder on the wood than in (2).
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two trains, Train A and Train B, are initially at rest next to each other at a train station. Train A leaves the station with a uniform acceleration of 0.30 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. 2.0 minutes later, Train B leaves the station in the same direction as Train A with a uniform acceleration of 0.50 m $\mathrm{s}^{-}$ $^{2}$.

How long does Train B take to catch up with Train A?
questions.stemText: Two trains, Train A and Train B, are initially at rest next to each other at a train station. Train A leaves the station with a uniform acceleration of 0.30 m s-2. 2.0 minutes later, Train B leaves the station in the same direction as Train A with a uniform acceleration of 0.50 m s- 2. How long does Train B take to catch up with Train A? A 6.9 s B 180 s C 210 s D 410 s

appearances.originalFile: grail:16130 2022 H2 CJC Physics Promo Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Uses two elapsed times in the displacement equations and solves for catch-up.
questions.misconception: Ignoring Train A's head start

explanation.body: Let $t$ be the time in seconds since Train B starts. Using $s=ut+\frac12at^2$, Train A travels $\frac12(0.30)(t+120)^2$ and Train B travels $\frac12(0.50)t^2$. Equating the displacements at catch-up gives $\frac12(0.30)(t+120)^2=\frac12(0.50)t^2$, so $t\approx410\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: This time is far too short for B to erase A's 120 s head start.
perOption.B: This is when the trains have equal speeds, while A is still ahead.
perOption.C: At 210 s, B's displacement from the station is still smaller than A's.
perOption.D: Correct. Both trains have travelled the same distance.

questions.stemText:
A rower is sitting on a boat in the middle of a calm lake.

Which of the following forces forms a Newton’s third law pair with the upthrust acting on the boat?

A  The weight of the boat alone.
B  The weight of the rower alone.
C  The combined weight of the boat and the rower.
D  The force of the boat on the lake’s water to displace some of the lake’s water.

stemImage.alt: Question 4: A rower is sitting on a boat in the middle of a calm lake. Which of the following forces forms a Newton’s third law pair with the upthrust acting on the boat?

appearances.originalFile: grail:10439 CJC.H2.PRELIM.2023.P1.QP

questions.difficultyReason: Students identify the two bodies involved in the upthrust interaction.
questions.misconception: Confusing balanced forces with a third-law pair

explanation.body: The lake water exerts an upward force on the boat. Its Newton’s third-law partner is the downward force the boat exerts on the water as it displaces some of it.

perOption.A: The boat’s weight is the Earth’s force on the boat.
perOption.B: The rower’s weight is the Earth’s force on the rower.
perOption.C: The combined weight balances the upthrust in equilibrium and acts on the boat and rower.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Water is ejected at a speed of 0.5 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ onto a wall from the nozzle of a hose with a diameter of 0.01 m. The density of water is 1000 kg $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

If the water does not rebound, what is the force exerted by the water on the wall?
questions.stemText: Water is ejected at a speed of 0.5 m s-1 onto a wall from the nozzle of a hose with a diameter of 0.01 m. The density of water is 1000 kg m-3. If the water does not rebound, what is the force exerted by the water on the wall? A 5.0 x $10^{-3}$ N B 2.0 x $10^{-2}$ N C 2.5 x $10^{-2}$ N D 7.9 x $10^{-2}$ N

appearances.originalFile: grail:14541 CJC 2024.H2.Phy.PRELIM.P1 - QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student must calculate mass flow, use momentum change per unit time, and identify the reaction force.
questions.misconception: Using diameter as radius

explanation.body: The force of the wall on the water is the mass flow rate $\rho Av$ times the change in velocity. Taking the incident direction as positive gives $F=(1000)\pi(0.005)^2(0.5)(0-0.5)=-0.0196\ \mathrm{N}$. Newton’s third law gives an equal and opposite force of $2.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{N}$ on the wall.

perOption.A: Uses a radius half the correct value, reducing the force by a factor of four.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the nozzle diameter squared as the cross-sectional area.
perOption.D: Uses the diameter as the radius in the circular area formula.

A particle accelerates from rest.

The graph shows the variation of the velocity v of the particle with time t.

Which graph shows the variation of the velocity v with the acceleration a of the particle?
questions.stemText: A particle accelerates from rest. The graph shows the variation of the velocity v of the particle with time t. Which graph shows the variation of the velocity v with the acceleration a of the particle? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: grail:19909 CJC.2025.H2.Phy.PRELIM.P1 Q paper

questions.difficultyReason: Read the slope of one graph and identify how a constant quantity appears on the other graph.
questions.misconception: Swapping the velocity and acceleration axes

explanation.body: The velocity–time graph has a positive, constant gradient, so the acceleration is constant. Velocity increases at this fixed positive value of $a$, giving a vertical line on the velocity–acceleration graph.

perOption.A: Shows acceleration increasing as velocity rises, with acceleration initially zero.
perOption.B: Shows both quantities increasing from zero, even though the initial velocity–time gradient is positive.
perOption.C: Holds velocity constant while varying acceleration.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A gas molecule of mass $m$ moves with velocity $v$ and collides elastically with a wall perpendicular to that direction.

If the molecule makes $N$ such collisions per second with the wall, what is the average force $F$ exerted by the molecule on the wall?
A $F=mvN$
B $F=2mvN$
C $F=\frac{mv^2}{2}$
D $F=\frac{mv}{N}$

stemImage.alt: Question 11: A gas molecule of mass m moves with velocity v and collides elastically with a wall perpendicular to that direction. If the molecule makes N such collisions per

appearances.originalFile: grail:19909 CJC.2025.H2.Phy.PRELIM.P1 Q paper

questions.difficultyReason: Account for the momentum reversal, then use collision rate and Newton’s third law.
questions.misconception: Omitting the momentum reversal

explanation.body: Taking motion towards the wall as positive, each elastic collision changes the molecule’s momentum by $\Delta p=-mv-(+mv)=-2mv$. By Newton’s third law, the force on the wall is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force on the molecule. With $N$ collisions per second, the average force on the wall has magnitude $N|\Delta p|=2mvN$.

perOption.A: Counts only the incoming momentum and omits the momentum of the rebound.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives the molecule’s kinetic energy, which has units of joules.
perOption.D: Divides by the collision rate and omits the factor of two from the reversal.

questions.stem:
A body is initially at rest on a horizontal frictionless table.

A force then acts on it that varies with time as shown.

Which graph represents the variation with time of the velocity of the body?
questions.stemText: A body is initially at rest on a horizontal frictionless table. A force then acts on it that varies with time as shown. force 0 0 time Which graph represents the variation with time of the velocity of the body? A velocity 0 0 time B velocity 0 0 time C velocity 0 0 time D velocity 0 0 time

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct link between constant force, constant acceleration and a linear velocity rise.
questions.misconception: Thinking velocity follows the force, or that the body stops when the force is removed

explanation.body: By $F_{\mathrm{net}}=ma$, the constant positive force produces constant acceleration, so velocity increases along a straight line. When the net force is zero, acceleration is zero and the velocity–time graph is horizontal.

perOption.A: Copies the force pulse and shows instantaneous changes in velocity.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Shows deceleration after the force has dropped to zero.
perOption.D: Shows increasing acceleration during a constant force.

questions.stem:
A lorry is pulling a cart of mass 600 kg with a rope at a constant speed along a straight horizontal road. The horizontal force resisting the motion of the cart is 40 N.

The lorry now accelerates at 0.15 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$.

What is the tension in the rope?
questions.stemText: A lorry is pulling a cart of mass 600 kg with a rope at a constant speed along a straight horizontal road. The horizontal force resisting the motion of the cart is 40 N. The lorry now accelerates at 0.15 m s-2. What is the tension in the rope? A 65 N B 100 N C 130 N D 195 N

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: One application of F = ma with resistive force included.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the resistive force or using only ma

explanation.body: The cart has a forward tension $T$ and a backward resistive force of $40\ \mathrm N$. Newton's second law gives $T-40=600(0.15)$, so $T=130\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: A tension of $65\ \mathrm N$ leaves only $25\ \mathrm N$ to accelerate the cart.
perOption.B: A tension of $100\ \mathrm N$ leaves only $60\ \mathrm N$ of net force.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: A tension of $195\ \mathrm N$ gives $155\ \mathrm N$ of net force, exceeding the required $90\ \mathrm N$.

[A block labelled mass $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ rests on a frictionless slope rising at $30^\circ$ above a dashed horizontal line.]

A $1.6\ \mathrm m$

questions.misconception: Using free-fall acceleration along the slope

explanation.body: The downhill force is $mg\sin30^\circ$, so $a=g\sin30^\circ$. From rest, $s=\tfrac12at^2=\tfrac12(9.81\sin30^\circ)(0.80)^2\approx1.6\ \mathrm m$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A body having uniform acceleration $a$ increases its velocity from $u$ to $v$ in time $t$.

Which expression would not give a correct value for the body’s displacement during time $t$?

A $ut+\frac12 at^2$
B $vt-\frac12 at^2$
C $\frac{(v+u)(v-u)}{2a}$
D $\frac{(v-u)t}{2}$

stemImage.alt: Question 3: A body having uniform acceleration a increases its velocity from u to v in time t. Which expression would not give a correct value for the body’s displacement d

appearances.originalFile: grail:9613 DHS 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must recognize equivalent forms of the uniform-acceleration equations.
questions.misconception: Using half the change in velocity as the average velocity.

explanation.body: Options A, B and C are valid displacement equations for uniform acceleration. D uses half the change in velocity where the average velocity should be $\tfrac12(u+v)$.

perOption.A: This is the valid constant-acceleration equation $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$.
perOption.B: This is the valid form $s=vt-\tfrac12at^2$.
perOption.C: This is the valid equation $s=(v^2-u^2)/(2a)$ written in factored form.
perOption.D: Correct. The expression uses the velocity difference to calculate the average.

A starts at positive displacement and falls steeply before flattening near zero.
B starts at positive displacement with an almost horizontal tangent and curves increasingly steeply down to zero.

questions.misconception: Drawing a horizontal displacement–time line for terminal velocity.

explanation.body: The gradient of the displacement–time graph gives the velocity. Once the sphere reaches terminal velocity, the graph becomes a straight line with a positive gradient because displacement is measured in the direction of the fall.

perOption.A: Starts with a nonzero speed that decreases towards zero, although the sphere is released from rest.
perOption.B: Shows a continually increasing speed with no steady terminal speed.
perOption.C: Levels off at zero speed, and its initial gradient indicates a nonzero release speed.
perOption.D: Correct. The gradient becomes constant and positive at terminal velocity.

If the weight of the book is the ‘action’ force, what is the ‘reaction’ force?
questions.stemText: A book of weight W is at rest on a table. A student attempts to state Newton’s third law by saying that ‘action equals reaction’. book table If the weight of the book is the ‘action’ force, what is the ‘reaction’ force? A The force W acting downwards on the Earth from the table. B The force W acting upwards on the book from the table. C The force W acting upwards on the Earth from the book. D The force W acting upwards on the table from the floor.

options.label: A
options.text: The force W acting downwards on the Earth from the table.

options.label: B
options.text: The force W acting upwards on the book from the table.

options.label: C
options.text: The force W acting upwards on the Earth from the book.

options.label: D
options.text: The force W acting upwards on the table from the floor.

questions.difficultyReason: The student must distinguish a gravitational third-law pair from the forces balancing on the book.
questions.misconception: Pairing the book’s weight with its normal force.

explanation.body: The book’s weight is Earth’s downward gravitational pull on the book. Its reaction is the book’s upward gravitational pull on Earth, also of magnitude $W$. The forces act simultaneously on different objects, and both are gravitational.

perOption.A: Pairs the book’s weight with a downward contact force from the table.
perOption.B: Uses the equal upward support force, which also acts on the book and comes from a different interaction.
perOption.C: Correct. The book pulls upward on Earth by gravity.
perOption.D: Uses a contact force on the table from a separate interaction.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An object is dropped, from rest, 10.0 m above the surface of some water.

Assuming negligible air resistance, what is the time taken to reach the water and the speed with which the object enters the water?

Option | Time / $\mathrm{s}$ | Speed / $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
A | 1.02 | 10.0
B | 1.02 | 14.0
C | 1.43 | 10.0
D | 1.43 | 14.0

stemImage.alt: Question 3: An object is dropped, from rest, 10.0 m above the surface of some water. Assuming negligible air resistance, what is the time taken to reach the water and the s

appearances.originalFile: grail:12961 DHS 2022 JC1 Promos Physics (Paper 1)

questions.difficultyReason: Students must use two constant-acceleration equations with zero initial speed.

questions.difficultyReason: The student must resolve tension in two directions and convert the resulting angle to the vertical.
questions.misconception: Reporting the angle to the horizontal.

explanation.body: Let $\theta$ be the angle of the tension to the horizontal. Vertical equilibrium gives $T\sin\theta=mg$, and forward acceleration gives $T\cos\theta=ma$. Thus $\tan\theta=g/a\approx2$, so $\theta=63.4^\circ$ and the angle to the vertical is $26.6^\circ$. The bob hangs backward so that the horizontal component of tension points forward.

perOption.A: A forward displacement would make the horizontal component of tension point backward.

questions.stemText: The rotor blades of a helicopter pushes air vertically downwards at a speed of 15 m s-1, with a mass flow rate of 2500 kg s-1. The helicopter rises with constant acceleration of 12.5 m s-2. What is the mass of the helicopter? A 1680 kg B 2500 kg C 3000 kg D 3750 kg

appearances.originalFile: grail:12812 EJC 2021 J1 H2 Promo P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student must calculate thrust from momentum flow and then account for weight in the helicopter’s force balance.
questions.misconception: Treating thrust as the resultant force

explanation.body: The upward lift equals the rate of change of momentum of the air, $\dot m_{\mathrm{air}}\Delta v$. For the helicopter, $ma=F_{\mathrm{lift}}-mg$, so $m(a+g)=\dot m_{\mathrm{air}}\Delta v$. Thus $m=(2500)(15)/(12.5+9.81)\approx1680\ \mathrm{kg}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Reads the mass flow rate of the air as the mass of the helicopter.
perOption.C: Divides the lift by the helicopter’s acceleration without subtracting its weight.
perOption.D: Dividing thrust by $g\approx10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ assumes the helicopter is in vertical equilibrium.

perOption.A: The increasing gradient would require the resultant force to increase.
perOption.B: The flattening curve would require the resultant force to decrease to zero.

perOption.B: Halves the total flight time before substituting it into the round-trip equation.

A The displacement is greatest when the velocity is zero. B The object changes direction when the acceleration is zero. C The displacement increases only when the acceleration is positive. appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires reading gradient and sign of a v–t graph rather than any calculation.
questions.misconception: Confusing zero acceleration with change of direction

explanation.body: The maximum speed occurs at a peak or trough of the velocity–time graph, where $a=dv/dt=0$. Direction changes when velocity changes sign, and displacement increases wherever velocity is positive.

perOption.A: At $t=T$ the velocity is zero and the displacement has returned to zero, although the interior zero crossing does coincide with maximum displacement.
perOption.B: Direction changes when $v$ changes sign, while $a=0$ at the velocity extrema.
perOption.C: Displacement increases whenever $v>0$, even if the acceleration is negative.
perOption.D: Correct. The greatest speed occurs at a horizontal tangent.

questions.stem:
A hot air balloon of total mass M is descending vertically with a constant acceleration of 2.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. For the hot air balloon to ascend with an upward acceleration of 4.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$, some mass needs to be removed.

Assuming the upward lift remains the same, what is the amount of mass that must be removed?
questions.stemText: A hot air balloon of total mass M is descending vertically with a constant acceleration of 2.0 m s–2. For the hot air balloon to ascend with an upward acceleration of 4.0 m s–2, some mass needs to be removed. Assuming the upward lift remains the same, what is the amount of mass that must be removed? A 0.14M B 0.43M C 0.57M D 0.86M

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Two applications of Newton's second law with a changing mass and careful sign handling.
questions.misconception: Ignoring direction of acceleration or forgetting the mass changes in the second case

explanation.body: Let $L$ be the lift. On descent, Newton’s second law gives $Mg-L=2M$, so $L=M(g-2)$. On ascent, for the remaining mass $M_1$, $L-M_1g=4M_1$, so $L=M_1(g+4)$. Equating the lifts gives $M_1=0.57M$, so the mass removed is $0.43M$.

perOption.A: Counts only the initial downward acceleration in the required change of acceleration.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives the mass remaining after removal.
perOption.D: Overstates the mass reduction by doubling the required fraction.

If the angle of inclination is increased to $20^\circ$, the acceleration of the trolley would be doubled. What is the frictional force, assumed to be the same in both cases, acting on the trolley? A 0.12 N B 0.41 N C 0.86 N D 4.9 N

stemImage.alt: Question 4: A trolley of mass 0.50 kg moves with a certain acceleration down a runway which is inclined to the horizontal at 15. If the angle of inclination is increased t

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf
grail:9639 NJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Needs two Newton's second law equations with the acceleration ratio, then solving simultaneously.
questions.misconception: Ignoring friction in one case or doubling the gravity component too

explanation.body: Along the runway at $15^\circ$, Newton’s second law gives $mg\sin15^\circ-f=ma$. At $20^\circ$, it gives $mg\sin20^\circ-f=2ma$. Doubling the first equation and subtracting the second eliminates $a$, giving $f=mg(2\sin15^\circ-\sin20^\circ)=0.86\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: This friction is too small to make the second net force twice the first.
perOption.B: This is the increase in the downhill component of weight, which equals $ma$ for the first incline.
perOption.C: Correct. This friction satisfies both force equations.
perOption.D: This is the trolley’s full weight and would exceed the downhill component on both inclines.

questions.stemText: Two small masses A and B are placed at the bottom and top of a smooth slope inclined at $30.0^\circ$ to the horizontal. At time $t = 0$, mass A is launched up the slope with an initial speed of $4.00\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ while mass B is released from rest at the top of the slope. The two masses collide at a point along the slope. [Diagram: right-angled slope at $30.0^\circ$, A at the bottom, B at the top] The length of the slope is $5.00\ \mathrm{m}$. At what time does the collision occur? A $0.681\ \mathrm{s}$ B $1.25\ \mathrm{s}$ C $1.50\ \mathrm{s}$ D $2.46\ \mathrm{s}$

stemImage.alt: Question 5: Two small masses A and B are placed at the top and bottom of a smooth slope inclined at 30.0 to the horizontal. At time t = 0, mass A is launched up the slope

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Best solved by noticing both masses share the same acceleration, so relative motion is uniform.
questions.misconception: Thinking the accelerations make the relative motion non-uniform

explanation.body: Let $a=g\sin30^\circ$ be the common downslope acceleration. At collision, A is $4t-\frac12at^2$ up from the bottom and B is $\frac12at^2$ down from the top. These displacements sum to $5.00\ \mathrm{m}$, so the acceleration terms cancel and $t=5.00/4.00=1.25\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Double-counts the effect of gravity on the closing motion by treating A as speeding up the slope.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses a time at which $4.00t=6.00\ \mathrm{m}$, greater than the initial separation.
perOption.D: Uses a time long enough for B to have already reached the bottom.

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs recognising that equal time intervals require heights in the ratio 1:4:9:16.
questions.misconception: Assuming equally spaced beads give equally spaced sounds

explanation.body: For a constant interval $T$, bead $n$ must fall for $nT$, so its starting height is $s=\frac12g(nT)^2$. The heights above the floor are therefore proportional to $0,1,4,9,16,\ldots$, as in D.

perOption.A: Spaces the beads more closely toward the ceiling, where the gaps need to be larger.
perOption.B: Uses equal height gaps, which give shorter time gaps at greater heights.
perOption.C: Increases the gaps but misses the square-number heights, starting with heights in the ratio $1:3$ instead of $1:4$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A camera drone of mass 1.20 kg hovers steadily above ground using four propellers. Each of the propellers pushes 0.50 kg of air vertically downward each second.

[Diagram: a quadcopter drone with four propellers on arms and a camera mounted underneath.]

Assume that the air above the propellers is stationary and that the drone remains level throughout.

What is the speed of the air leaving each propeller?

A $1.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$   B $2.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$   C $5.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$   D $24\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 4: A camera drone of mass 1.20 kg hovers steadily above ground using four propellers. Each of the propellers pushes 0.50 kg of air vertically downward each second.

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must link the thrust to the rate of change of momentum of the air and share the weight among four propellers.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to share the weight among the four propellers

explanation.body:
Since the drone hovers steadily and stays level, each propeller provides an equal share of the weight:

thrust per propeller $= \dfrac{1.20 \times 9.81}{4} = 2.943\ \mathrm{N}$

By Newton's second law, $F = \dfrac{dp}{dt} = \dfrac{m}{t}(v - 0)$, where $\dfrac{m}{t} = 0.50\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$ for each propeller:

$2.943 = 0.50\,v \Rightarrow v = 5.886 \approx 5.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Gives the drone's mass value (1.2) rather than calculating a speed.
perOption.B: Takes the thrust per propeller (2.94 N) as the answer without dividing by the mass flow rate.
perOption.C: Correct. Thrust per propeller = (mass flow rate) $\times$ $v$.
perOption.D: Uses the drone's whole weight for one propeller instead of sharing it among four.

Rain falls vertically downwards and enters an open container fixed securely to the car at a constant rate of $0.50\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$. After entering the container, the rainwater moves horizontally with the car.

What is the horizontal force exerted by the container on the car as a result of collecting the rain?

A. $0\ \mathrm{N}$
B. $5.0\ \mathrm{N}$
C. $10\ \mathrm{N}$
D. $20\ \mathrm{N}$

stemImage.alt: Question 3: A car is travelling in a straight horizontal line at a constant speed of 20 m s−1. Rain falls vertically downwards and enters an open container fixed securely t

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires applying the momentum-rate form of Newton's second law to incoming rain at constant car speed.
questions.misconception: Assuming constant car speed means the collected rain requires no force

explanation.body: The collected rain gains horizontal momentum at the rate $F=\frac{d(mv)}{dt}=v\frac{dm}{dt}=(20)(0.50)=10\ \mathrm{N}$. The container therefore exerts a $10\ \mathrm{N}$ backward force on the car as the rain pushes back on it.

perOption.A: Ignores the horizontal momentum gained by the rain.
perOption.B: Underestimates the force by using less than the full horizontal velocity gain at the given mass flow rate.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Omits the factor of $0.50$ from the mass flow rate.

questions.stemText:
X and Y are two objects on a frictionless table connected by a string. The mass of X is $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ and the mass of Y is $4\ \mathrm{kg}$. The mass of the string is negligible. A constant horizontal force of $12\ \mathrm{N}$ acts on Y.

[On a horizontal table, block X ($2\ \mathrm{kg}$) is to the left of block Y ($4\ \mathrm{kg}$). A horizontal string joins them, and a $12\ \mathrm{N}$ arrow points right from Y.]

What are the acceleration of Y and the magnitude of the tension in the string?

Acceleration of Y / $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, tension in the string / $\mathrm{N}$
A 2, 4
B 2, 6
C 3, 4
D 3, 6

stemImage.alt: Question 3: X and Y are two objects on a frictionless table connected by a string. The mass of X is 2 kg and the mass of Y is 4 kg. The mass of the string is negligible. A

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires applying Newton’s second law to the pair and then to one block.
questions.misconception: Applying the full pulling force to Y alone

explanation.body: For the two blocks together, $F_{\mathrm{net}}=ma$ gives $12=(4+2)a$, so $a=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. For X, the tension is the net horizontal force, so $T=2(2)=4\ \mathrm{N}$. Using Y gives the same result from $12-T=4(2)$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: The acceleration is right, but the tension is the force needed to accelerate the $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ block, giving $4\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.C: The tension is right, but dividing $12\ \mathrm{N}$ by Y’s mass alone ignores X.
perOption.D: Dividing by Y’s mass alone ignores X, and the tension must equal X’s mass times the common acceleration.

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising that the separation grows with the square of time for two cars starting from rest.
questions.misconception: Assuming separation grows linearly with time

explanation.body: For cars starting from rest, $s=\tfrac12at^2$ and $s'=\tfrac12a't^2$. At $3\ \mathrm{s}$, $12=\tfrac12(9)(a'-a)$, giving $a'-a=\tfrac83\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. At $6\ \mathrm{s}$, the separation is $\tfrac12(36)(\tfrac83)=48\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the separation by treating the added time as a fixed increment instead of applying the square-time relation.
perOption.B: Doubles the separation as if it were proportional to time.
perOption.C: Triples the separation, though doubling the time multiplies it by four.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stem: An electric train consists of two carriages, each of mass 1.0 x $10^{5}$ kg. The motor, which is in the front carriage, provides a constant traction force of 1.2 x $10^{5}$ N. Assume that all resistive forces are negligible. The train accelerates from rest. After 20 s, the coupling between the two carriages breaks. How far apart are the carriages after another 20 s?
questions.stemText: An electric train consists of two carriages, each of mass 1.0 x 105 kg. The motor, which is in the front carriage, provides a constant traction force of 1.2 x 105 N. Assume that all resistive forces are negligible. The train accelerates from rest. After 20 s, the coupling between the two carriages breaks. How far apart are the carriages after another 20 s? A 120 m B 240 m C 360 m D 480 m

appearances.originalFile: grail:10482 TJC 2023 H2 Prelim Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: Chained kinematics: the front carriage's acceleration changes after the coupling breaks.
questions.misconception: Forgetting that the front carriage's acceleration doubles once the rear one is shed

explanation.body:
At the start: $1.2\times10^5 = 2(1.0\times10^5)a$, so $a = 0.60\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. At $t=20\ \mathrm{s}$, $v = 0.60\times20 = 12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

The back carriage then moves at constant $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$: in 20 s it travels $240\ \mathrm{m}$.

The front carriage now has $a = 1.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$: $s = 12(20)+\tfrac12(1.2)(20)^2 = 480\ \mathrm{m}$.

Separation $= 480-240 = 240\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Not obtained from the correct motion of either carriage.
perOption.B: Correct. Front 480 m minus back 240 m.
perOption.C: Not obtained from the correct motion of either carriage.
perOption.D: This is the distance travelled by the front carriage alone, not the separation.

Friction on mass $M$ is $f$ and $f$ is proportional to $M$. What is the magnitude of the force that $3M$ exerts on $2M$? A $F/2$. B $F/2+3f$. C $F/3+f$. D $F/3+3f$.

questions.difficultyReason: Apply Newton's second law to the system, then to a single block, with friction proportional to mass.
questions.misconception: Ignoring that friction scales with each block's mass

explanation.body:
Whole system: $F-6f = 6Ma$, so $a = \dfrac{F-6f}{6M}$ (friction is proportional to mass: $f$, $2f$, $3f$).

For block $3M$: $F_1 - 3f = 3Ma$, so $F_1 = 3M\left(\dfrac{F-6f}{6M}\right)+3f = \dfrac F2$.

perOption.A: Correct. The friction terms cancel.
perOption.B: Adds $3f$ to $F/2$ again; friction on $3M$ is already included.
perOption.C: Splits $F$ equally between the three blocks.
perOption.D: Splits $F$ equally between the three blocks and adds friction wrongly.

A device for spraying paint consists of a box with its axes horizontal and vertical. One of its vertical faces contains small holes. Paint is fed into the box under pressure via a vertical tube and exits through the holes as fine horizontal streams.

The paint is ejected at a speed of 3.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ through 27 holes, each of area 0.4 $\mathrm{mm}^{2}$. The density of the paint is 900 kg $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

What is the horizontal force required to hold the device stationary as it ejects the paint?

Paint is fed into the box under pressure via a vertical tube and exits through the holes as fine horizontal streams. The paint is ejected at a speed of 3.0 m s–1 through 27 holes, each of area 0.4 mm2. The density of the paint is 900 kg m–3. What is the horizontal force required to hold the device stationary as it ejects the paint? A 21 m N B 29 mN C 44 m N D 87 m N

questions.difficultyReason: Needs mass flow rate from density, area and speed, then force as rate of change of momentum, with unit conversion of mm$^2$.
questions.misconception: Forgets that mass flow rate itself contains $v$, so uses $F = \rho A v$.

explanation.body:
Force equals rate of change of momentum of the paint: $F = N\rho A v^2$.

$F = (27)(900)(0.4\times10^{-6})(3.0)^2 = 0.087\ \mathrm{N} = 87\ \mathrm{mN}$.

perOption.A: Does not match the calculation; likely a slip in the number of holes or a missing factor.
perOption.B: Does not match the calculation; probably an arithmetic or unit slip.
perOption.C: Does not match the calculation; probably an arithmetic or unit slip.
perOption.D: Correct. $F = \rho A v^2$ per hole, times 27 holes.

|---|---|---|
| A | 7.1 | 7.1 |
| B | 7.1 | 10 |
| C | 10 | 7.1 |

questions.difficultyReason: Requires area under a v–t graph with a negative region and distinguishing distance from displacement.
questions.misconception: Treating area below the time axis as positive displacement

explanation.body:
Displacement = area under the v–t graph, with area below the time axis counted as negative: $\frac{1}{2}(2+10)(20) - \frac{1}{2}(10)(4) = 120 - 20 = 100\ \mathrm{m}$.

Average velocity $= \dfrac{100}{14} = 7.1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.B: Swaps the two: speed uses distance (140 m), velocity uses displacement (100 m).

explanation.body:

questions.stemText:
A goods train passes through a station at a steady speed of $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. An express train is at rest at the station. The express train leaves the station with a uniform acceleration of $0.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ just as the goods train goes past. Both trains move in the same direction on straight, parallel tracks.

How much time passes before the express train overtakes the goods train?

A 6.0 s  B 10 s  C 20 s  D 40 s

stemImage.alt: Question 2: A goods train passes through a station at a steady speed of 10 m s−1. An express train is at rest at the station. The express train leaves the station with a un

appearances.originalFile: grail:10487 YIJC 2023 H2Phy Prelim P1 Question Paper

questions.difficultyReason: A standard equal-displacement kinematics problem with one quadratic.
questions.misconception: Taking the overtaking moment as when the speeds are equal

explanation.body:
The express train overtakes the goods train at time $t$ when both have the same displacement from the station.

Goods train: $s_1 = ut = 10t$

Express train: $s_2 = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(0.50)t^2$

Setting $s_1 = s_2$: $10t = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.50)t^2$, so $t = 40\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Not the time at which the two displacements are equal.
perOption.B: Not the time at which the two displacements are equal; at 10 s the express train has covered only 25 m against the goods train's 100 m.
perOption.C: This is when the two trains have equal speeds (or results from dropping the ½ in $\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$); the express train is still behind at that moment.
perOption.D: Correct. Equal displacements give $10t = 0.25t^2$.

explanation.body:

Its Newton's third law (action–reaction) partner acts on the other body, the back wheel, and is the forward push of the road on the back wheel.

questions.stem:
Two blocks of mass 2.0 kg and 5.0 kg are connected by a light string that is passed over a frictionless pulley. The 2.0 kg block is accelerating up the slope.

Given that the friction between the block and the surface of the slope is 7.0 N, what is the tension in the string?
questions.stemText: Two blocks of mass 2.0 kg and 5.0 kg are connected by a light string that is passed over a frictionless pulley. The 2.0 kg block is accelerating up the slope. 5.0 kg 30 Given that the friction between the block and the surface of the slope is 7.0 N, what is the tension in the string? A 26 N B 31 N C 39 N D 49 N

appearances.originalFile: grail:10487 YIJC 2023 H2Phy Prelim P1 Question Paper

questions.difficultyReason: Needs a connected-body analysis with an incline component and friction in two steps.
questions.misconception: Taking tension equal to the hanging weight even when the system accelerates

explanation.body:
Consider the whole system (7.0 kg) along the string:

$\Sigma F = ma$: $(5)(9.81) - (2)(9.81)\sin 30^\circ - 7.0 = 7a$, so $a = 4.61\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

Now the 5.0 kg block alone: $(5)(9.81) - T = 5(4.61)$, so $T = 26\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The hanging block accelerates downward, so $T < 5g$.
perOption.B: Not consistent with the system's acceleration of $4.61\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; check the forces on each block.
perOption.C: Too large; the tension must be less than the 49 N weight by $ma = 23\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.D: Equals the weight of the 5.0 kg block, which would only hold if it were not accelerating.

A $6.0 \times 10^{2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ B $1.2 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ C $6.0 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ D $1.2 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:14610 YIJC 2024 JC2 PRELIM H2 Phy P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Two chained kinematics equations with a unit conversion.

explanation.body:
During free fall: $v = u + at = 0 + (-9.81)(1.0) = -9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

On hitting the sand: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, so $0 = (-9.81)^2 + 2a(8.0\times10^{-3})$, giving $a = -6.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

The average deceleration is $6.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: A power-of-ten slip when converting 8.0 mm to metres.
perOption.B: Uses $v$ instead of $v^2$, or another arithmetic slip; $v^2/2s$ gives about $6\times10^3$.
perOption.D: Omits the factor of 2 in $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.

questions.stem: A car of mass 1500 kg has a driving force of 5600 N and it pulls a trailer of mass 500 kg. The resistive forces acting on the car and trailer are 1200 N and 400 N respectively. What is the tension in the coupling between the car and trailer for this acceleration?
questions.stemText: A car of mass 1500 kg has a driving force of 5600 N and it pulls a trailer of mass 500 kg. The resistive forces acting on the car and trailer are 1200 N and 400 N respectively. What is the tension in the coupling between the car and trailer for this acceleration? A 0 N B 1400 N C 1800 N D 2600 N

appearances.originalFile: grail:14610 YIJC 2024 JC2 PRELIM H2 Phy P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Standard two-body connected system: find common acceleration, then isolate the trailer.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to include resistive forces when isolating one body

explanation.body:
Treat car and trailer as one system: $F_{net} = 5600 - 1200 - 400 = 4000\ \mathrm{N}$, so $a = \frac{4000}{1500+500} = 2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

Now consider the trailer alone: $F_{net} = m_{trailer}a = 500(2.0) = 1000\ \mathrm{N}$.

Since $F_{net} = T - f_{trailer}$: $1000 = T - 400$, so $T = 1400\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: The trailer accelerates against a 400 N resistance, so the coupling must pull on it.
perOption.B: Correct. $T = m_{trailer}a + f_{trailer} = 1000 + 400$.
perOption.C: Finds the acceleration ignoring all resistive forces ($2.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$), then adds the trailer's resistance.
perOption.D: Applies Newton's second law to the car but forgets the car's own 1200 N resistance ($5600 - 1500 \times 2.0$).
